opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons. The most basic one is just reliability. When you have a closed-form solution, like we do with LEACE, our least-squares concept erasure method, you're not relying on gradient descent or some adversarial training loop that might or might not converge. A lot of the earlier concept erasure work used adversarial approaches: you train a classifier to detect the concept, then you train the representation to fool that classifier, and you go back and forth. Those setups are notoriously finicky. They can look like they've removed the information when really they've just found a configuration where that particular adversary fails, and a fresh probe can still recover the concept.

With a closed-form solution, you can actually prove things. For LEACE, we can show that after erasure, no linear classifier can do better than a constant predictor at recovering the concept. That's a real guarantee, not just an empirical observation on a test set. And on top of that, the solution is optimal in a precise sense: among all the transformations that achieve that guarantee, it changes the representation as little as possible in a least-squares sense. So you're doing the minimum damage to everything else the model knows.

There's also a practical side. It's cheap. You compute some covariance statistics, you do some linear algebra, and you're done. That means you can apply it at every layer of a large language model. We had a procedure called concept scrubbing that does exactly that. If each layer required its own expensive adversarial training run, that just wouldn't scale.

And then, from more of a scientific or interpretability standpoint, closed-form solutions are understandable. You can look at the formula and see why it works. It connects to things like whitening and orthogonal projection, so it's not a black box. If we're trying to understand neural networks, I think it's nice when our tools for studying them aren't themselves opaque neural networks. You want at least some of your instruments to be things you can reason about mathematically.

r001.rationale: The response says LEACE avoids relying on gradient descent or adversarial training, and describes the closed-form procedure as cheap to compute.

r002.rationale: It says closed-form methods let you prove guarantees, then states that LEACE is optimal among transformations meeting the guarantee and minimizes representation changes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the big thing for me is that a closed form solution lets you actually understand what's going on. When you're doing something like concept erasure, the usual approach is adversarial: you train a classifier to detect the concept, you train something else to fool it, and you go back and forth. And at the end you have a thing that maybe works, but you don't really know why it works, you don't know if it's converged to something meaningful, and you can't guarantee anything about it. It's this iterative, kind of hacky process, and it's sensitive to hyperparameters and random seeds and all of that.

With LEACE, what we showed is that if you just want to prevent any linear classifier from recovering the concept, there's a unique minimal change to your representations that does it, and you can write it down. It's a projection plus a whitening-type transformation, and that's it. You compute some covariance matrices and you're done. So you get a guarantee, not an empirical "well, the probe accuracy went down to chance on this one test set." You can prove that no linear probe, no matter how it's trained, can do better than chance.

And then the other thing is it's just cheap. You don't need gradient descent, you don't need to train anything, you can run it on a huge model in a few seconds. That matters practically, because if you want to apply this at every layer of a model, or do it at inference time, you can't be running an adversarial training loop for each one.

But honestly, I think the deeper reason I care is that closed form solutions tend to tell you something about the structure of the problem. When you can get one, it usually means you've found the right way to frame things. And the places where you can't get one are informative too, because they tell you where the real difficulty is, like the nonlinear case, where you have to start making assumptions about the function class.

r001.rationale: The response says the method requires no gradient descent or training and can run in a few seconds.

r002.rationale: It describes the change as uniquely minimal and says linear probes can be proven unable to recover the concept, but does not clearly state that the closed-form solution comes with a proof of its optimality.

astra-6.text: I think a closed-form solution is useful because it gives you something you can inspect directly. Instead of running an optimization procedure and trying to infer why it produced a particular result, you can look at the expression and ask how the solution depends on the assumptions or the data. That can make it easier to see which parts of the problem actually matter. It doesn’t necessarily mean the solution is cheap to compute, but it can give you a much clearer starting point for understanding what’s going on.

r001.rationale: It contrasts inspecting a closed-form expression with running an optimization procedure, but does not say this avoids computationally intensive optimization such as gradient descent.

r002.rationale: It does not state that a closed-form solution comes with a proof of optimality.

sol-6.1.text: A closed-form solution can make it much easier to understand what a method is actually doing. With an iterative algorithm, you have to think about the objective, the optimizer, whether it converges, and how all those choices interact. If you can write the answer down directly, you can often see which properties of the data determine the result and which assumptions matter. It can also be faster to compute, although closed form doesn’t automatically mean computationally cheap. For me, the main benefit is that it gives you something concrete to reason about.
